analysis.investment_thesis: INOX India is a genuinely excellent cryogenic equipment business — high ROCE, near-zero debt, secular tailwinds from LNG and hydrogen — but at 41x EV/EBITDA with FCF turning negative, the price already reflects a decade of perfection. When everyone agrees the story is wonderful and the stock has more than doubled from its Dec-2023 IPO price, the bet is no longer on the business but on whether the next buyer is more optimistic than you.
key_strengths: ROCE of 38% and near-debt-free balance sheet (D/E 0.10) signal a capital-light, competitively protected niche
Diversified end-market exposure — LNG, green hydrogen, ISRO/space, ITER fusion — provides multiple secular growth vectors
Consistent OCF positive all 5 years with expanding operating margins (~22%), demonstrating pricing power
key_risks: 41x EV/EBITDA with FCF effectively zero (-3 Cr in FY25) leaves zero margin of safety if growth disappoints even modestly
Net profit CAGR of only 2.7% over 6 years despite 12.3% revenue growth — earnings conversion is structurally weak; 'other income' and tax effects inflate reported PAT
Capex tripled from 44 Cr (FY22) to 125 Cr (FY25) while OCF stayed flat at ~122 Cr — the business is consuming cash during a heavy investment phase with uncertain payback timing
red_flags: Stock at 2.3x its Dec-2023 IPO price (₹660→₹1,492) — euphoric re-rating driven by hydrogen/space narrative, not earnings
Consensus uniformly bullish on green hydrogen theme — classic Marks warning sign when everyone agrees
Free cash flow yield is essentially 0% on a ₹13,539 Cr market cap — no current return; investor is paying entirely for optionality
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The second-level question here isn't 'is INOX India a good business?' — it clearly is. The question is: what must be true for INR 1,492 to be justified? At 41x EV/EBITDA on INR 301 Cr of EBITDA, reaching a reasonable 20x multiple in five years requires EBITDA to roughly double to ~600 Cr, implying revenue of ~3,000 Cr at current margins — an 18%+ CAGR from a base that grew at 12% over the prior six years. That's not impossible, but it is priced-to-perfection with zero tolerance for cycle slowdown, project delays, or margin compression. The IPO was sold in December 2023 near a market peak; the stock has since more than doubled on narrative momentum — exactly the dynamic Marks describes when sellers (promoters at 75% lock-in) time their exits with peak optimism.

The financial deterioration in FCF is the most important signal the market is ignoring. OCF has been stuck at ~120-130 Cr for three years while capex surged from 44 Cr to 125 Cr — the business is in a heavy-investment phase, and the returns on that capital are unproven. Net profit CAGR of 2.7% over six years tells you that earnings power has barely moved in absolute terms; the ROE/ROCE shine because the equity base is small, not because profits are compounding rapidly. In a stress scenario — LNG cycle softens, green hydrogen deployment delays (likely given policy execution risk in India), or interest rates stay elevated — this stock could re-rate to 20-25x EV/EBITDA, implying 40-50% downside. That asymmetry — capped upside, severe downside — is precisely the unfavorable risk/reward I avoid.
